title: Password Cracker
directAnswer: Decide whether the login attempt can be split into a sequence of the given passwords (each reusable any number of times), and if so reconstruct that sequence. This is the Word Break problem with path reconstruction: scan from the front, and at each position try every password that matches as a prefix, recursing on the remainder. The key to making it fast is memoising the positions from which no valid split exists, so each suffix is explored once. Output the passwords space-separated, or "WRONG PASSWORD" if no split works. O(N · K · L) time where N = attempt length, K = number of passwords, L = max password length.

remember.pattern: Word Break (segmentation) with memoised suffixes and path reconstruction
remember.formula:
canSplit(start):
    if start == len(attempt): return []   # empty suffix → success
    if start in failed: return null       # memoised dead end
    for pw in passwords:
        if attempt.startsWith(pw, start):
            rest = canSplit(start + len(pw))
            if rest != null: return [pw] + rest
    failed.add(start)                     # remember this start fails
    return null
rules: Memoise **failed start indices**, not just visited ones — without it, overlapping prefixes (e.g. `a`, `aa`) cause exponential re-exploration.
Passwords may be **reused** any number of times — it's unbounded segmentation, so don't 'consume' a password.
Match must be **anchored** at the current index (`startsWith(pw, start)`), and a successful split must consume the string **exactly** to the end.
On total failure print exactly `WRONG PASSWORD` (uppercase, single space) — a formatting slip fails the test.
Greedily taking the first matching password is wrong; you must be able to backtrack when a choice leads to a dead end.
whenToUse: Can a target string be segmented into pieces drawn from a dictionary?
Pieces are reusable and you need either a yes/no or one valid segmentation
Overlapping prefixes make greedy matching fail and demand backtracking
You can phrase progress as 'consume a valid prefix, recurse on the rest'
antiSignals: Each piece may be used at most once → bitmask / assignment DP, not free segmentation
You need ALL segmentations enumerated → backtracking without the pruning power of plain memo (count can be exponential)
Pieces can overlap in the target (not a clean concatenation) → different model
The dictionary is enormous and pieces long → build a trie/Aho–Corasick for prefix matching
remember.takeaway: Segmentation problems collapse to 'consume a matching prefix, recurse on the remainder'. The single optimisation that turns exponential into polynomial is memoising the start indices that fail — once a suffix is known unsplittable, never re-enter it.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise this as Word Break, see why greedy prefix matching fails, and add memoisation on failed start positions to avoid exponential blow-up — plus careful reconstruction and output formatting.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Greedily taking the first matching password without backtracking, forgetting to memoise failed indices (TLE on inputs like passwords {a, aa, aaa} with attempt aaaa...b), or mis-formatting the WRONG PASSWORD output.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Show a concrete input where greedy fails, derive the recursion, explain that memoising failed suffixes makes it O(N·K·L), and note the bottom-up DP with parent pointers as an iterative alternative.

problemStatement:
There are `n` users registered on a website, each with a known password. The passwords are given as a list of lowercase strings. An attacker has concatenated some of these passwords (each may be used any number of times, in any order) into a single login attempt string with no separators.

Given the list of passwords and the login attempt, determine whether the attempt can be formed by concatenating passwords. If it can, return the sequence of passwords (in order, space-separated) that forms it; otherwise return the string `WRONG PASSWORD`.
constraints: 1 ≤ length of the login attempt ≤ 2000 (concatenation of one or more passwords)
All strings are lowercase English letters; passwords are reusable
understanding: We must tile the login attempt left to right using passwords as tiles, where any tile can be reused. At each boundary we try every password that matches starting there and recurse on what's left. The trap is greed: the first password that matches a prefix might lead to a dead end later, while a different (possibly shorter or longer) matching password would succeed. So we need backtracking. The efficiency trap is recomputation: many distinct prefixes can lead to the same suffix start index, so we memoise which start indices are hopeless and never revisit them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a password be used more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — any password may appear any number of times. This makes it free (unbounded) segmentation rather than a one-use assignment problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If multiple segmentations exist, which do I return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any one valid segmentation is accepted. We return the first one our search finds.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What exactly is printed on failure?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The literal string `WRONG PASSWORD` (uppercase, one space). Mismatched casing or spacing fails the judge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could two passwords share a prefix, breaking greedy matching?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — e.g. passwords {ab, abc} on attempt 'abcd...'. Greedily taking 'ab' may strand the rest, while 'abc' succeeds. That's why backtracking is required.

examples.input: passwords = [because, can, do, must, we, what], attempt = "wedowhatwemustbecausewecan"
examples.output: we do what we must because we can
examples.explanation: The attempt splits cleanly into we|do|what|we|must|because|we|can, reusing 'we' three times.
After matching 'hello', the remaining 'world' matches no password, and there's no alternative split — so it's unformable.

Greedily taking 'ab' first leaves 'cd' which works too (ab|cd), but the single password 'abcd' is also a valid split. Either 'ab cd' or 'abcd' is acceptable; the search returns whichever it finds first.
No combination of a/aa/aaa ever produces the trailing 'b'. This is the classic input that blows up without memoising the failing start index.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Backtracking Without Memo (Exponential)
approaches.whenToMention: State it to establish the recursive structure and to show a concrete blow-up case, then add memoisation.
hints: From the current index, try every password that matches the string starting there; for each, recurse on the index just past it.
If the index reaches the end, you've consumed the whole attempt — success; bubble the chosen passwords back up.
On adversarial inputs like passwords {a, aa, aaa} and attempt 'aaaa...ab', the same suffix index is reached through many prefix combinations, so this recomputes exponentially.
approaches.complexityReasoning: With K passwords, each position can branch K ways and the depth is up to N, so the search tree is exponential. Overlapping prefixes mean the same start index is re-explored along many paths.
approaches.explanation:
Define `solve(start)` = a list of passwords whose concatenation equals `attempt[start..]`, or `null` if impossible.

**Recursion.** If `start` equals the length, the suffix is empty and we succeed with an empty list. Otherwise, for each password `pw`, if `attempt` starts with `pw` at position `start`, recurse on `solve(start + pw.length())`. If that returns a list (not null), prepend `pw` and return. If no password leads to success, return `null`.

**Why greed fails (and why this backtracks).** Taking the first matching password unconditionally can strand the remainder. Consider passwords `{ab, abc}` and attempt `abcd` where only `cd` is also a password: greedily matching `ab` then `cd` works, but if `cd` were absent and only `d`+something worked via `abc`, greed on `ab` would dead-end. Backtracking tries the next password whenever a branch fails, so it never gets stuck on a bad first choice.

**Why it's exponential.** Inputs like `{a, aa, aaa}` with `aaaa…ab` let countless prefix combinations land on the same suffix start, each re-explored from scratch. The cure is to remember which start indices are hopeless — the next approach.
approaches.insight: The recursion is correct on its own; the disaster is purely repeated work. The same suffix start index gets re-derived through exponentially many prefix paths — exactly the overlapping-subproblem signature that says 'memoise me'.

approaches.name: Memoised Backtracking on Failed Suffixes (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'same recursion, but cache the start indices that can't be split'.
hints: Add a set 'failed' of start indices already proven unsplittable; bail out immediately if the current start is in it.
Because there are only N+1 distinct start indices, each is fully explored at most once — that's what bounds the work.
Per index you try K passwords, each requiring an O(L) prefix comparison, giving O(N·K·L) overall.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are N+1 start indices. Each is processed once (subsequent visits short-circuit via the failed set). Processing an index tries K passwords with O(L) match checks → O(N·K·L) time, O(N) for the memo and recursion depth.
approaches.explanation:
Take the brute-force recursion and add one cache: a set `failed` of start indices from which no valid split exists.

**The change.** At the top of `solve(start)`, if `start ∈ failed`, return `null` instantly. Before returning `null` (no password worked), insert `start` into `failed`. That single memo guarantees each start index is fully expanded at most once.

**Why caching *failures* is enough.** Successes return immediately and unwind the whole stack, so a successful index is never revisited. Only failing indices get re-reached (through different prefix paths), so caching just the failures is sufficient — and it's exactly the set that caused the exponential blow-up.

**Complexity.** With the memo, the work is bounded by (number of start indices) × (work per index) = `(N+1) × (K passwords × O(L) prefix check)` = `O(N·K·L)`. For N ≤ 2000, K ≤ 10, L ≤ 10 that's tiny.

**Reconstruction.** When a recursive call returns a non-null list, prepend the password we matched and propagate up. The top-level call returns the full ordered list, which we join with spaces; `null` becomes `WRONG PASSWORD`.
approaches.insight: You don't need to memoise everything — only the dead ends. Successful paths self-prune by returning straight to the top, so a set of failing start indices is the minimal cache that kills the exponential behaviour.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up DP with Parent Pointers
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the iterative, stack-safe alternative — fills a reachability array and reconstructs from back-pointers.
hints: Let reachable[i] mean 'attempt[i..] up to some boundary is splittable starting at i'. Work the other way: dp[i] = can attempt[0..i) be split.
dp[0] = true. For each end i, if dp[j] is true and attempt[j..i) is a password, set dp[i] = true and record parent[i] = j (and which password).
If dp[N] is true, walk parent pointers from N back to 0 to rebuild the password sequence, then reverse it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Outer loop over N end positions, inner over K passwords with O(L) comparison → O(N·K·L). Arrays dp and parent are O(N); reconstruction is O(N).
approaches.explanation:
Recast the recursion as a forward DP over prefix lengths, avoiding recursion entirely.

**State.** `dp[i]` is true iff `attempt[0..i)` (the first `i` characters) can be segmented into passwords. `dp[0] = true` (empty prefix).

**Transition.** For each end index `i` from 1 to N, look at each password `pw`. If `pw` ends exactly at `i` (i.e. `i ≥ len(pw)` and `attempt[i-len..i) == pw`) and `dp[i-len]` is true, then `dp[i]` is true. Record `parent[i] = i - len` and `chosen[i] = pw` so we can rebuild the path.

**Reconstruction.** If `dp[N]` is true, start at `i = N`, repeatedly emit `chosen[i]` and jump to `parent[i]` until reaching 0, then reverse the collected passwords. Otherwise output `WRONG PASSWORD`.

**Why prefer it sometimes.** It's iterative (no deep recursion on long attempts), and the reachability array makes the logic easy to reason about. Same asymptotic cost as the memoised recursion; pick whichever reads more clearly for you.
approaches.insight: Word Break has a clean forward formulation: a prefix of length i is splittable iff some earlier splittable prefix is followed by a password ending at i. Storing one parent pointer per index turns the yes/no DP into a path-reconstructing one for free.

pitfalls: Forgetting to reverse the reconstructed list — back-pointers yield it end-to-front.
Using `break` but then needing ALL segmentations — break only gives one (which is all this problem wants).
Indexing s.startsWith at the wrong offset (use i-len, the password's start).

commonMistakes: Greedily taking the first matching password without backtracking.
Omitting memoisation of failed start indices — exponential time on overlapping-prefix inputs.
Mis-formatting the failure output (must be exactly 'WRONG PASSWORD').

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Greedy first-match without backtracking
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Committing to the first password that matches can strand the rest of the string even when another split succeeds. You must try alternatives on failure.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No memoisation of dead ends
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without caching failed start indices, inputs like {a, aa, aaa} on 'aaaa…ab' re-explore the same suffix exponentially and time out.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong failure string
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The judge expects the exact token 'WRONG PASSWORD'. Lowercase, extra spaces, or a different message fails even when the logic is correct.

patternNote: Password Cracker is Word Break with path reconstruction. Model it as 'consume a matching prefix, recurse on the rest', backtrack on dead ends, and memoise the start indices that fail to turn exponential search into O(N·K·L). The iterative dp[i]+parent-pointer formulation is the stack-safe equivalent.
